paragraphs_over6.paragraph: The FX record describes one market maker, while the weekly series combine signed positions across primary dealers. The weekly experiment replays a fixed downloaded vintage on economic-date indices. It stipulates that current and earlier snapshot values are known at each issue, making the current-position floor known under that replay convention. Public release occurs later; these inputs therefore define an idealized information set rather than a historical public observer's information (Federal Reserve Bank of New York(n.d.)) . The reporting definitions identify the positions being aggregated. Each analysis uses its own units, training history, forecast horizon, and issue grid, with reference rules matched inside the relevant comparison. The data design makes frequency and measurement differences visible instead of treating every sequence as an interchangeable dealer history.

Conditional-regression loss against same-history historical headroom on a logarithmic (c=W/(H+1) ) axis; this coordinate excludes coefficient count. Light marks distinguish discovery and confirmation simulations, while dark marks distinguish the financial tasks; the lower panels repeat a labelled detail range. Bands summarize the discovery simulation's post hoc first-cutpoint envelopes, and dashed lines mark its point estimates. Of the FX curve predictions, three identified cutpoints agree with their prespecified intervals, while the remaining case stays untestable through left censoring. Both longer-horizon curves lose again at the largest history, and the universal simplification criterion fails in the confirmation experiment. Repeated FX cells use the same period. Discovery cutpoints interpolate the raw coordinate across pooled horizons; financial crossings interpolate raw history within a horizon. Their consistency supports a partial history pattern, with horizon collapse and coefficient normalization remaining unidentified.

writing.abstract_text: Peak-position limits concern the largest absolute inventory reached before a review ends, making completed path labels and the observed current position central to forecasting. We compare historical and conditional quantile reports for an FX market maker and weekly primary-dealer position aggregates, using matched histories and update schedules. Simple historical rules remain demanding benchmarks across frequencies, position categories and reference choices. At the shorter horizon, long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8% and 16.6% in the previously reported later and earlier windows. A post hoc history-to-horizon display summarizes pooled simulation tasks, and a new simulation passes its prespecified history-region screens. Retrospective FX curves partly agree with the resulting cutpoint bands, while censoring, large-history reversals and failed universal simplification limit that evidence. For limit managers, these findings motivate matching completed-label histories before assessing conditional forecasts jointly on score, breaches and stability.
